title: Class 5 Maths Money: Bills, Budgets, Profit & Loss (with Case Studies + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Money: Bills, Budgets & Profit
meta_desc: Class 5 maths money made simple: read bills, plan a budget, use the unitary method, and handle profit, loss and decimals. Worked case studies + free quiz.
excerpt: Money is the one chapter your Class 5 child will use the same afternoon they learn it. Here is how to teach bills, budgets, the unitary method and simple profit and loss the way it actually shows up at the shop, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a ten-year-old a ₹100 note at the kirana shop and watch what happens. They can name the coins, but ask them whether ₹100 covers two packets of biscuits at ₹28 each, a ₹15 chocolate and a ₹24 pen, and the counting slows right down. That gap — between recognising money and reasoning with it — is exactly what the class 5 maths money chapter is meant to close. It is the most practical topic in the whole year, because a child uses it the same afternoon they learn it.

Over the years I have found Class 5 money splits cleanly into four skills: reading a bill and adding it up, planning a budget, working out costs with the unitary method, and handling simple profit, loss and discount. Get those four solid and the rest is just neat handwriting. Let us take them in the order a child meets them at a real shop.

Reading a bill and totalling it

A bill is really just a small addition table with rupees and paise. The one rule I drill hardest: keep the decimal points in a straight line, so rupees sit under rupees and paise under paise. A misplaced point turns ₹45.50 into ₹455.0, and the child hands over ten times too much.

ItemRateQuantityAmount
Notebook₹32.003₹96.00
Pencil box₹45.501₹45.50
Eraser₹4.752₹9.50
Total₹151.00

Notice the eraser line: ₹4.75 × 2 = ₹9.50, not ₹8.150. Multiplying money with paise trips up more children than any other single thing in this chapter, so slow down there.

Money with decimals: rupees and paise

One hundred paise make one rupee, which means every rupee amount is just a decimal. So ₹7 and 50 paise is written ₹7.50, and 5 paise is ₹0.05, not ₹0.5. I teach children to always fill two places after the point — ₹9.5 should be written ₹9.50 — because on a bill the two paise columns must line up.

  • ₹1 = 100 paise
  • 75 paise = ₹0.75
  • ₹12.05 = 12 rupees and 5 paise (not 50 paise)
  • ₹250 − ₹175.50 = ₹74.50 change

Planning a budget

A budget answers one question: does the money coming in cover the money going out? Give a child a fixed amount — say a ₹500 monthly pocket money — and a wishlist that adds up to more, and let them cut items until it fits. That decision, choosing what to drop, is the real lesson. It is also where the idea of ‘money left over’ (savings) first lands, which matters more than any sum on the page.

Case study 1: Riya’s birthday budget

Riya has ₹500 to spend on her birthday party. She buys a cake for ₹250, party hats for ₹60, and wants two bottles of juice at ₹45 each. Can she also buy a return gift costing ₹120?

Add up what she has committed: cake ₹250 + hats ₹60 + juice (₹45 × 2 = ₹90) = ₹400. Money left = ₹500 − ₹400 = ₹100. The return gift costs ₹120, so the answer is no — she is short by ₹20. Either she drops one juice bottle to free up ₹45, or she chooses a gift under ₹100. This is a genuine budgeting choice, and Class 5 children argue about it happily.

The unitary method: cost of many from cost of one

The unitary method is the workhorse of class 5 maths money, so it earns its own drill. The idea is two clean steps: first find the cost of one unit, then multiply for the number you want.

If 6 pens cost ₹90, one pen costs ₹90 ÷ 6 = ₹15, so 4 pens cost ₹15 × 4 = ₹60. Always find the value of one first — children who skip that step and try to jump straight to the answer are the ones who get muddled. The counter-intuitive bit to point out: dividing first, then multiplying, feels like more work but is far less error-prone than guessing a shortcut.

Simple profit, loss and discount

Shopkeepers buy at one price (cost price) and sell at another (selling price). If they sell higher, that is profit; if lower, a loss. Keep the language plain at this level — no percentages needed unless your child is ready.

  • Profit = Selling Price − Cost Price
  • Loss = Cost Price − Selling Price
  • Discount = the amount taken off the marked price

Case study 2: Arjun’s lemonade stall

Arjun spends ₹120 on lemons, sugar and cups to make 40 glasses of lemonade. He sells each glass for ₹5. On a hot Sunday he sells all 40. What is his profit? He collects 40 × ₹5 = ₹200. His cost was ₹120, so profit = ₹200 − ₹120 = ₹80. Now the honest twist: if only 20 glasses sold, he collects ₹100, which is less than his ₹120 cost — a ₹20 loss. Same stall, different day. That is a real trade-off, and it teaches why shopkeepers worry about selling out.

faq.q: What does the Class 5 maths money chapter actually cover?
faq.a: It covers reading and totalling bills, adding and subtracting rupees and paise as decimals, planning a simple budget, the unitary method (finding the cost of many from the cost of one), and simple profit, loss and discount — all in Indian rupees.

faq.q: What is the unitary method in simple words?
faq.a: First find the cost of a single item, then multiply for the quantity you want. If 6 pens cost ₹90, one pen is ₹90 ÷ 6 = ₹15, so 4 pens cost ₹15 × 4 = ₹60. Always find the value of one first.

faq.q: How do I stop my child making mistakes with paise?
faq.a: Write every amount with two digits after the decimal point (₹9.50, not ₹9.5) and keep the points in a vertical line when adding a bill. Most paise errors come from a stray or misaligned decimal point.

faq.q: Do Class 5 children need to learn profit and loss with percentages?
faq.a: No. At Class 5, keep it to rupees only: profit is selling price minus cost price, loss is cost price minus selling price. Percentage-based profit and loss comes in later grades.
